topics.title: Network fundamentals and performance terms
topics.oneLine: A network moves data through links and devices; performance is about how much useful data arrives and how long it takes.
topics.whyItMatters: GATE-style Network questions often hide a simple calculation behind words such as rate, delay, bottleneck, or packet size. This topic gives you the vocabulary and the calculation order.
understandSimply: A network has end systems (phones, PCs, servers), links (copper, fibre, radio) and forwarding devices (switches and routers). Data is usually cut into packets so many users can share the same links.

Do not treat bandwidth, throughput and goodput as synonyms. Bandwidth is the link's maximum carrying capacity. Throughput is the rate actually delivered. Goodput is only useful application data delivered per second; headers and retransmitted bytes do not count.

analogy.title: Useful analogy
analogy.text: Think of a highway. Lane capacity is bandwidth, cars that actually arrive per minute are throughput, and passengers reaching the destination are goodput.

technicalExplanation: Packet switching shares a link packet by packet. It is efficient for bursty computer traffic but packets can wait in queues. Circuit switching reserves a path for a call; capacity is predictable but can sit idle. A virtual circuit is a logical, preselected path in a packet network: packets carry an identifier and normally follow that path.

A packet can experience processing delay at a node, queueing delay before a busy link, transmission delay while its bits enter a link, and propagation delay while its signal travels. Queueing is often the most variable term, but processing, transmission and propagation can change too when hardware, packet size, link rate or path changes. For multiple hops, add the relevant delay terms for every link and intermediate node.

definitions.definition: Maximum data rate supported by a link, in bit/s.
Rate at which data is successfully delivered over a path.
Useful application payload delivered per second, excluding protocol overhead and retransmissions.
Variation in packet delay; high jitter harms real-time audio/video.
Slowest resource limiting end-to-end throughput.

steps.title: Solve a delay question
steps.description: Write packet length L in bits, rate R in bit/s, distance d in metres and propagation speed s in m/s. Then list every link and intermediate node mentioned.

steps.title: Add only relevant terms
steps.description: Use L/R for each transmission, d/s for each propagation, then add stated processing or queueing delays.

steps.title: Interpret the result
steps.description: Ask whether the question wants first-packet latency, steady-state throughput, or data that can be in flight.

formulasAndMethods: Transmission delay = L/R. It is time to put all L bits onto one link.
Propagation delay = d/s. It is time for a signal to travel distance d.
End-to-end delay across n links = sum of transmission and propagation delays, plus relevant processing and queueing at nodes.
Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth × RTT. It estimates how many bits can be in flight before the first acknowledgement returns.

comparisons.title: Switching choices
rows: Predictable capacity; idle reservation wastes capacity
Ordered path state; still packet based

solvedExamples.question: A 12,000-bit packet enters a 6 Mbit/s link. What is its transmission delay?
solvedExamples.solution: L/R = 12,000 ÷ 6,000,000 = 0.002 s = 2 ms. This is not the propagation delay.

solvedExamples.question: A 2,000 km fibre path has propagation speed 2×10^8 m/s. Find propagation delay.

traps: A higher bit rate reduces transmission delay, not propagation delay.
Goodput is not link capacity; protocol headers and retransmissions reduce it.
For a multi-hop path, do not calculate only one link unless the question says so.
takeaways: Bandwidth is capacity; throughput is achieved delivery rate; goodput is useful payload rate.
Transmission delay depends on packet size and link rate.
Propagation delay depends on distance and signal speed.
Bottleneck capacity limits steady-state throughput.
Bandwidth-delay product means data that can fill a path.

quickRecall.question: Which delay changes when packet size doubles on the same link?
What does goodput exclude?
What does the bandwidth-delay product represent?
quickRecall.answer: Approximate bits that can be in flight over a path.

topics.title: OSI and TCP/IP models
topics.oneLine: Layering lets each part of a network solve one job while hiding unnecessary detail from the layer above.
topics.whyItMatters: Layer, header and PDU questions are quick marks only if you can follow one message from an app to the wire and back.
understandSimply: A protocol is the rulebook used by peer entities at the same layer. A service is what one layer offers to the layer above. For example, IP offers best-effort delivery to TCP; TCP does not need to know the details of Ethernet framing.

The OSI model is a seven-layer reference model. The Internet protocol suite is usually taught as four layers: Application, Transport, Internet and Link; some books split Link into Data Link and Physical to make five layers.
technicalExplanation: OSI layers from top to bottom are Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link and Physical. The Internet model maps Application to the top three OSI layers, Transport to Transport, Internet to Network, and Link to Data Link plus Physical. Encryption can be applied at more than one layer; do not force every security question into Presentation.

Encapsulation adds control information while data travels downward. Application data becomes a TCP segment or a UDP datagram, then an IP packet (often also called an IP datagram), then a link-layer frame. A link-layer trailer, such as Ethernet FCS, may be added. At the receiver, decapsulation removes the outer headers/trailer in reverse order.

definitions.definition: Rules for message format, order and action between peer entities.
Function a layer makes available to the layer above.
Wrapping higher-layer data with a layer's header and sometimes trailer.
Protocol data unit; its name depends on the layer and protocol.

steps.title: Follow a web request
steps.description: Application creates message; TCP or UDP adds transport control; IP adds source/destination addresses; Ethernet adds local-link addresses and FCS.

steps.title: At a router
steps.description: The incoming Ethernet frame is removed. The IP packet is examined, then placed in a new frame for the next link.

steps.title: At the receiver
steps.description: Each layer checks/removes its information and passes the payload upward to the intended application.

formulasAndMethods: Layer-identification method: MAC/FCS → Link; IP address/TTL → Internet/Network; port/sequence number → Transport; URL/DNS/SMTP command → Application.
PDU reminder: TCP normally uses segment; UDP commonly uses datagram; IP uses packet or datagram; Ethernet uses frame.

solvedExamples.question: A device chooses an outgoing path using an IP prefix. Which layer is being used?
solvedExamples.solution: Network/Internet layer. IP addresses and routing are Internet-layer functions.

solvedExamples.question: A UDP application sends one message. What is the usual transport PDU name?
solvedExamples.solution: A UDP datagram, not a TCP segment. “Segment” is specific to TCP in normal terminology.

traps: Protocol is not the same as service.
A router changes link-layer frames at every hop but normally forwards the IP packet onward.
Do not call all transport PDUs segments.
takeaways: OSI explains functions; TCP/IP is the Internet protocol suite.
Headers identify/control each layer's work.
Encapsulation goes down; decapsulation goes up.
Ports are transport-layer identifiers; IP addresses are Internet-layer identifiers.
TCP segment and UDP datagram are different names for a reason.

quickRecall.question: Which layer contains TCP/UDP ports?
What happens to an Ethernet header at a router?
quickRecall.answer: It is removed and replaced for the next link.

quickRecall.question: Name the seven OSI layers from top to bottom.
quickRecall.answer: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical.

sources.title: GATE 2026 CS syllabus — Section 10
usedFor: Scope: layering, OSI and TCP/IP stacks

topics.title: Hub, repeater, bridge, switch, router and gateway
topics.oneLine: Devices differ mainly in what they inspect and where they stop a collision or broadcast.
topics.whyItMatters: Device, collision-domain and broadcast-domain questions are common because a single word—hub, VLAN or router—changes the answer.
understandSimply: A repeater works with signals: it regenerates a weak signal. A hub is a multiport repeater, so it repeats incoming bits to every other port. Neither understands MAC or IP addresses.

A bridge and a Layer-2 switch inspect MAC addresses. A router inspects IP prefixes and connects different IP networks. Gateway is context dependent: a default gateway is usually the local router, while an application gateway may translate between unlike protocols.
technicalExplanation: A bridge/switch learns source MAC-to-port mappings and forwards or filters frames using destination MAC addresses. It divides collision domains: in the usual exam model, every active switch port is a separate collision domain. Modern switched Ethernet is normally full duplex, so collisions do not occur on those links; the exam phrase describes the segment boundary, not an everyday collision event.

A Layer-2 broadcast stays inside its VLAN. A VLAN creates separate Layer-2 broadcast domains on one physical switch. A router normally does not forward a LAN broadcast between interfaces, so each routed interface is the edge of a broadcast domain.

definitions.definition: Shared medium on which simultaneous transmissions could collide.
Set of interfaces reached by a Layer-2 broadcast.
Logical Layer-2 LAN that creates a separate broadcast domain.
Router a host uses to reach off-subnet destinations.

steps.title: Identify the device
steps.description: Bits only: repeater/hub. MAC address: bridge/switch. IP prefix: router.

steps.title: Count collision domains
steps.description: In an exam diagram, count active switch ports/segments; a hub and its attached hosts share one.

steps.title: Count broadcast domains
steps.description: Count distinct VLANs or router-separated Layer-2 networks.

formulasAndMethods: Device test: forwarding by MAC address → bridge/switch; forwarding by IP prefix → router.
Domain test: switches split collision domains; routers and VLANs split broadcast domains.

comparisons.title: Networking devices
rows: Separate collision domains; broadcast stays in VLAN

solvedExamples.question: Eight hosts connect one per port to a switch. How many collision domains in the usual exam model?
solvedExamples.solution: Eight, one per switch port. In modern full-duplex Ethernet the ports do not normally suffer collisions, but the ports remain separate segments.

solvedExamples.question: A switch has VLAN 10 and VLAN 20. How many Layer-2 broadcast domains?
solvedExamples.solution: Two. Broadcast traffic in VLAN 10 is not flooded into VLAN 20 without routing or a Layer-3 device.

traps: A plain switch does not stop broadcasts inside the same VLAN.
A hub does not learn addresses.
Default gateway does not mean DNS server or every kind of protocol gateway.
takeaways: Hub repeats bits; switch forwards frames; router forwards packets.
Switches learn source MACs and use destination MACs.
VLANs split broadcast domains at Layer 2.
Routers normally stop Layer-2 broadcasts.
Full-duplex Ethernet removes normal collisions, not the conceptual port boundary.

quickRecall.question: Which address does a switch use to learn a table entry?
What separates broadcast domains on a switch?
quickRecall.answer: Different VLANs, or routing between networks.

quickRecall.question: What does a default gateway usually mean?
quickRecall.answer: The local router used for off-subnet traffic.

topics.title: Ethernet, MAC addressing and switching
topics.oneLine: Ethernet delivers frames on one LAN, and a switch learns where MAC addresses live before deciding whether to forward, flood or filter.
topics.whyItMatters: Frame-field and switch-table questions reward a fixed two-step method: learn the source first, then look up the destination.
understandSimply: An Ethernet frame is a local-link container. Its destination MAC tells the switch where the frame should go on this LAN; its source MAC lets the switch learn where the sender was seen. These MAC addresses are not the same job as end-to-end IP addresses.

A switch does not know every MAC address initially. It builds its forwarding table by observing incoming frames. If it does not know a destination, it sends an unknown unicast to all other ports in the VLAN so the destination has a chance to reply.
technicalExplanation: At exam depth, an Ethernet frame has a destination MAC, source MAC, type/length field, payload and a Frame Check Sequence (FCS). The FCS is a CRC-based error-detection value. It can reveal damage; it does not repair a frame or guarantee delivery.

After learning the source, the switch looks up the destination. A known unicast is sent only to the learned outgoing port. An unknown unicast and a broadcast are flooded to every other port in the VLAN. If the destination table entry points to the same port the frame arrived on, the switch filters it: sending it back would be pointless. CSMA/CD is relevant to old shared, half-duplex Ethernet. It is not used for ordinary full-duplex switched links.

definitions.definition: Link-layer address; Ethernet commonly uses 48 bits.
Frame Check Sequence used to detect corruption in a frame.
Frame whose destination MAC has a learned output port.
Unicast destination absent from the forwarding table.

steps.title: Learn
steps.description: Record incoming source MAC → ingress port; update the entry if the source moves.

steps.title: Look up
steps.description: Find destination MAC in the forwarding table.

steps.title: Act
steps.description: Known different port: forward. Unknown/broadcast: flood except ingress. Same ingress port: filter.

formulasAndMethods: A 48-bit MAC address is 12 hexadecimal digits because 48 ÷ 4 = 12.
Switch-table method: source is learned; destination decides the output action.

comparisons.title: Switch forwarding outcomes
rows: Flood except ingress port within VLAN

solvedExamples.question: A frame enters port 3 with source A and destination B. Table already has B → port 3. What happens?
solvedExamples.solution: The switch learns/refreshes A → port 3, then filters the frame because B is also on the ingress port.

solvedExamples.question: Why are 12 hexadecimal digits enough for a usual Ethernet MAC address?
solvedExamples.solution: Each hex digit represents 4 bits. 12 × 4 = 48 bits.

traps: Learning uses source MAC; forwarding lookup uses destination MAC.
FCS detects corruption but does not retransmit or correct the frame.
CSMA/CD is not a feature of a normal full-duplex switch port.
takeaways: Ethernet is Link-layer delivery, not end-to-end routing.
MAC addresses are usually 48 bits.
Learn source, look up destination.
Unknown unicast and broadcast are flooded within a VLAN.
Same-port destination is filtered.

quickRecall.question: What does FCS do?
quickRecall.answer: It detects corrupted Ethernet frames using a check value.

quickRecall.question: When does a switch flood an unknown unicast?
quickRecall.answer: When it has no destination-MAC table entry, except it never sends it back on ingress.

quickRecall.question: When is CSMA/CD relevant?
quickRecall.answer: Shared, half-duplex Ethernet; not normal full-duplex switched Ethernet.

topics.title: Error detection, flow control and sliding-window protocols
topics.oneLine: Error detection notices damaged data; ARQ protocols use acknowledgements and retransmissions to recover; windows keep sender and receiver in step.
topics.whyItMatters: This topic combines short numerical questions on sequence space with conceptual GBN-versus-SR questions.
understandSimply: A parity bit detects any odd number of flipped bits, but misses an even number. A checksum combines data words and is simple but weaker than CRC for many burst errors. CRC treats bits as a polynomial and appends a remainder so the receiver can check for likely corruption.

Flow control stops a fast sender overwhelming a slower receiver. At the data link, it controls frames across one link. TCP flow control is end-to-end and uses the receiver's advertised window; it is not the same as congestion control, which protects the network.
technicalExplanation: Stop-and-Wait sends one frame, then waits for an ACK or timeout. Stop-and-Wait ARQ retransmits after loss/corruption. Sliding-window protocols allow several outstanding frames, keeping a high-delay link busy. A sender window limits what may be sent without acknowledgement; a receiver window tells which sequence numbers it can accept.

Go-Back-N (GBN) uses cumulative acknowledgements and normally accepts only the next expected frame. After a loss, it retransmits that missing frame and later outstanding frames. Selective Repeat (SR) buffers acceptable out-of-order frames and retransmits only missing ones. With m-bit sequence numbers, GBN sender window is at most 2^m−1; SR window is at most 2^(m−1) to avoid confusing an old frame with a wrapped new one.

definitions.definition: Automatic Repeat reQuest: reliability using ACKs, timeouts and retransmission.
Number of bit positions in which two codewords differ.
Acknowledgement of all data up to a point.
Range of sequence numbers a sender may send or receiver may accept.

steps.title: Detect
steps.description: Receiver checks parity, checksum or CRC. A bad frame is not accepted as good data.

steps.title: Acknowledge
steps.description: Receiver ACKs correctly received sequence information; sender advances its window.

steps.title: Recover
steps.description: On timeout/loss, Stop-and-Wait retransmits one; GBN retransmits a suffix; SR retransmits selected missing frames.

formulasAndMethods: GBN maximum sender window = 2^m−1 for m-bit sequence numbers.
SR maximum window = 2^(m−1).
Minimum distance d detects up to d−1 errors and corrects floor((d−1)/2) errors.

solvedExamples.question: With 3-bit sequence numbers, what is the maximum GBN sender window?
solvedExamples.solution: 2^3−1 = 7. The 8 sequence values cannot all be outstanding because wraparound would be ambiguous.

solvedExamples.question: A code has minimum Hamming distance 5. How many bit errors can it correct?
solvedExamples.solution: floor((5−1)/2) = 2. It can detect up to 4 errors.

traps: Error detection alone does not retransmit data.
GBN and SR are both sliding-window protocols, but only SR buffers out-of-order frames.
Data-link flow control is hop-by-hop; TCP receive-window flow control is end-to-end.
takeaways: Parity, checksum and CRC detect; ARQ recovers by retransmission.
Stop-and-Wait has one outstanding frame.
Sliding windows pipeline frames.
GBN retransmits a suffix; SR retransmits selectively.
SR window is at most half the sequence space.

quickRecall.question: What does a cumulative ACK acknowledge?
quickRecall.answer: All correctly received data up to the acknowledged point.

quickRecall.question: Which protocol buffers out-of-order frames?
What is GBN's maximum sender window with m sequence bits?

sources.title: RFC 1122 — Communication Layers
usedFor: Reliable delivery and window terminology context

topics.title: IPv4 addressing
topics.oneLine: IPv4 gives a 32-bit address to an interface and adds a header that routers use to deliver packets and limit their lifetime.
topics.whyItMatters: Questions mix address fields, TTL, fragmentation and special ranges. Keeping this topic separate from subnet arithmetic prevents careless mistakes.
understandSimply: An IPv4 address has 32 bits, usually written as four decimal octets. A prefix length says how many leading bits name the network; the rest identify a host/interface in that network. Detailed subnet range calculations come next in Topic 7.
An IPv4 router forwards packets toward a destination address. It does not promise reliable, ordered delivery—that is work for higher layers such as TCP.
technicalExplanation: Exam-relevant IPv4 header fields include version, header length, total length, identification, flags, fragment offset, TTL, protocol, header checksum, and source/destination addresses. TTL is reduced at forwarding hops; a packet whose TTL reaches zero is discarded, preventing endless loops. Protocol identifies the payload type such as TCP, UDP or ICMP.

If a packet is too large for an outgoing link's MTU and fragmentation is allowed, IPv4 can split it. Identification lets the destination group fragments; the More Fragments flag tells whether more follow; fragment offset states a fragment's position in the original payload in 8-byte units. The destination reassembles fragments. A Don't Fragment setting prevents router fragmentation; an oversized packet is then discarded and may trigger ICMP feedback.

definitions.definition: Internet Protocol version 4, using 32-bit addresses.
Time To Live field; reduced by routers to limit packet lifetime.
Maximum transmission unit: largest packet/frame payload a link can carry without fragmentation at that layer.
Addressing a host itself; IPv4 loopback block is 127.0.0.0/8.
Addresses reserved for private networks: 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16.

steps.title: Read an IPv4-header question
steps.description: First decide whether it asks delivery (destination address), loop prevention (TTL), payload type (Protocol) or fragmentation.

steps.title: For fragmentation
steps.description: Keep the same identification for related fragments; use flags/offset to locate each fragment.

steps.title: For ranges
steps.description: Recognise 127/8 as loopback and RFC 1918 private-use blocks before applying any subnet mask.

formulasAndMethods: IPv4 address length = 32 bits = four octets.
Network address = IP address bitwise AND subnet mask.
Fragment offset is measured in 8-byte units, not ordinary bytes.

solvedExamples.question: A packet begins with TTL 3 and crosses three routers. Can it be delivered after the third forwarding decision?
solvedExamples.solution: No. Each router reduces TTL; when it reaches zero, the packet is discarded rather than forwarded onward.

solvedExamples.question: Why can fragments from two packets be kept apart at the destination?
solvedExamples.solution: Fragments carry an Identification value; with source, destination and protocol context it identifies fragments belonging to one original datagram.

traps: TTL is not a measure of physical time left; routers decrement it per hop in normal practice.
IP header checksum covers the IPv4 header, not the entire payload.
172.15.x.x is not in the 172.16/12 private-use block.
takeaways: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits.
Prefix separates network and host portions.
TTL prevents packets circulating forever.
Identification, flags and offset support fragmentation.
Private, loopback and multicast ranges have special meanings.

quickRecall.question: Which IPv4 field prevents indefinite routing loops?
What unit is IPv4 fragment offset measured in?
Is 172.15.1.1 private-use?

topics.title: Subnetting, CIDR and route aggregation
topics.oneLine: Subnetting divides an address block; CIDR describes flexible prefixes; routers choose the most specific matching prefix.
topics.whyItMatters: Subnetting is one of the highest-return calculation areas. A repeatable method beats memorising individual masks.
understandSimply: A mask or /prefix marks the network bits with leading 1s. Everything after the prefix is the host portion. In a normal IPv4 LAN subnet, all-zero host bits give the network address and all-one host bits give the directed broadcast address.

Subnetting borrows host bits to create smaller networks. VLSM means giving different-sized subnets to different needs rather than forcing every subnet to be equal. CIDR removed old class boundaries and lets any valid prefix length describe a block.
technicalExplanation: For /p, the block has 2^(32−p) addresses. In ordinary subnets that reserve network and broadcast addresses, usable hosts are 2^(32−p)−2. Exceptions exist: /31 point-to-point links and /32 host routes are purposeful special cases, so follow the question's stated assumptions.

Longest-prefix match means a router chooses the matching route with the greatest prefix length. For aggregation, combine only contiguous, correctly aligned blocks with shared leading bits. For example, 192.0.2.0/24 and 192.0.3.0/24 aggregate to 192.0.2.0/23 because the /23 begins on an even third octet and covers both.

definitions.definition: 32-bit mask whose leading 1s identify the prefix.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing; variable-length prefix notation.
Variable Length Subnet Masking; using different subnet sizes in one allocation.
Choose the matching route with the most prefix bits.
Advertise adjacent aligned blocks as one shorter prefix.

steps.title: Find a subnet range
steps.description: Convert /prefix to mask or block size. Find the block containing the IP. First address is network; last is broadcast; addresses between are usable under ordinary rules.

steps.title: Create equal subnets
steps.description: Borrow b bits: number of subnets = 2^b; new prefix = old prefix + b.

steps.title: Do VLSM
steps.description: Sort host requirements largest first, allocate the smallest fitting power-of-two block, then continue from the next boundary.

formulasAndMethods: Addresses in /p = 2^(32−p).
Traditional usable hosts = 2^(32−p)−2 when network and broadcast are reserved.
Block size in one changing octet = 256 − mask value in that octet.
For equal subnets, borrow b bits to obtain 2^b subnets.

solvedExamples.question: Find network, broadcast and ordinary host range for 192.0.2.77/26.
Split 10.0.0.0/24 into four equal subnets.
solvedExamples.solution: Need 2 bits because 2^2=4. New prefix /26. Networks start at 10.0.0.0, .64, .128 and .192.

traps: /24 is a larger block than /26, not a smaller one.
Do not choose a route only by metric before checking longest prefix.
Aggregation needs both contiguity and alignment; two nearby-looking blocks may not form one exact prefix.
takeaways: Prefix length counts network bits.
Network is IP AND mask.
Block size finds a range quickly.
VLSM allocates largest requirements first.
Longest matching prefix wins in routing lookup.

quickRecall.question: How many ordinary usable hosts does /27 have?
Which route wins: 10.0.0.0/8 or 10.1.0.0/16 for destination 10.1.2.3?
What is the aggregate of 192.0.2.0/24 and 192.0.3.0/24?

sources.title: RFC 4632 — CIDR Address Assignment and Aggregation

topics.title: ARP, DHCP, ICMP and NAT
topics.oneLine: These support protocols solve different practical problems: local address resolution, configuration, control/error reporting and address translation.
topics.whyItMatters: The same words—address, request, reply—appear in several protocols. Exam questions reward knowing which layer and which address each one handles.
understandSimply: ARP solves one local-LAN question: “I know the IPv4 address of my next hop; what MAC address should I put in this Ethernet frame?” It does not resolve names and it does not cross routers.

DHCP gives a host configuration such as IP address, mask, default gateway and DNS server. ICMP carries IP control/error messages. NAT changes addresses at a boundary; PAT/NAPT also changes transport ports so many internal flows can share one public address.
technicalExplanation: For a same-subnet destination, a host ARPs for the destination host's MAC. For a remote destination, it keeps the remote IP as the IP destination but ARPs for the default router's local-interface MAC. This is a classic IP-versus-MAC distinction.

The initial DHCP sequence is Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge (DORA). ICMP examples include Echo Request/Reply used by ping, Destination Unreachable and Time Exceeded. NAT is not encryption or authentication; it is address translation. PAT uses address plus port translation to identify many conversations.

definitions.definition: Address Resolution Protocol: maps a local IPv4 next-hop address to a link-layer address.
Time-limited configuration assignment to a client.
Internet Control Message Protocol for IP diagnostics and error reporting.
Network Address Translation, changing IP address information across a boundary.
NAT that also translates TCP/UDP identifiers such as ports.

steps.title: Send to another subnet
steps.description: Host compares destination with its own prefix, chooses default gateway, ARPs for gateway MAC, builds Ethernet frame to gateway, and retains remote IP destination.

steps.title: Get a DHCP lease
steps.description: Client broadcasts Discover; server Offers; client Requests one offer; server Acknowledges configuration.

steps.title: Read a diagnostic
steps.description: ICMP describes an IP-layer condition; it is carried inside IP, not TCP or UDP.

formulasAndMethods: DORA: Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge.
Address test: DNS maps name → address; ARP maps local IPv4 next hop → MAC; NAT maps addresses across a boundary.

comparisons.title: Protocol roles
rows: IPv4 to MAC on one link

solvedExamples.question: A host sends to 203.0.113.8 through its default router. Whose MAC appears as Ethernet destination on the first LAN?
solvedExamples.solution: The default router's local-interface MAC. The IP destination remains 203.0.113.8.

solvedExamples.question: Put initial DHCP messages in order.
solvedExamples.solution: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge. The offer must come before the client requests that offered configuration.

traps: ARP does not map domain names; DNS does.
ICMP is neither TCP nor UDP.
NAT can hide private addresses but does not itself provide confidentiality.
takeaways: ARP is local-link IPv4-to-MAC resolution.
Off-subnet traffic ARPs for the gateway, not remote host.
DHCP DORA provides configuration.
ICMP reports/control diagnostics for IP.
PAT adds port translation to NAT.

quickRecall.question: What does ARP resolve for a remote destination?
quickRecall.answer: The default gateway's local IP address to its MAC address.

quickRecall.question: Name one ICMP message used by traceroute-style hop expiry diagnostics.
What extra identifier does PAT translate in addition to address?
quickRecall.answer: A transport identifier, commonly a TCP or UDP port.

sources.title: GATE 2026 CS syllabus — Section 10
usedFor: Scope: ARP, DHCP, ICMP and NAT

topics.title: Routing algorithms and routing protocols
topics.oneLine: Routing learns or computes paths; forwarding is the fast per-packet act of using the resulting table.
topics.whyItMatters: Questions often mix an algorithm with a named protocol. Anchor your answer on who knows the topology, what is exchanged and whether it is inside or between autonomous systems.
understandSimply: A router receives a packet, looks up the destination prefix in its forwarding table, and sends the packet to a next hop. That lookup is forwarding. Routing is the slower control-plane process that fills and updates the table.

Shortest-path routing chooses a least-cost path. Flooding sends a packet on all suitable outgoing links; it is robust but wasteful, so sequence numbers or hop limits are used. Different routing algorithms distribute enough information for routers to make choices.
technicalExplanation: Distance-vector routers tell neighbours their best known distance to destinations and use the Bellman-Ford update. Bad news can travel slowly, creating count-to-infinity; split horizon and poisoned reverse help limit this. Link-state routers flood link-state information so each router builds a topology map and runs Dijkstra's algorithm locally.

RIP is an interior distance-vector protocol with hop count as a metric. OSPF is an interior link-state protocol. BGP is used between autonomous systems and applies policy/path attributes, including AS_PATH; it is not simply a shortest-hop algorithm. Regardless of how routes were learned, packet forwarding uses longest-prefix match among matching entries.

definitions.definition: Data-plane table mapping destination prefixes to next hops/outgoing interfaces.
Neighbour-to-neighbour exchange of destination cost estimates.
Flooded topology information followed by local shortest-path computation.
Networks under one administrative routing policy.
Slow increase of an unreachable route's metric in distance-vector routing.

steps.title: Forward one packet
steps.description: Match destination address against table prefixes, choose the longest match, then send to listed next hop/interface.

steps.title: Distance vector
steps.description: Receive neighbour distances, add local link cost, choose minima, advertise changes.

steps.title: Link state
steps.description: Discover local links, flood advertisements, build common map, run Dijkstra.

formulasAndMethods: Bellman-Ford update: D_x(y) = min_v { c(x,v) + D_v(y) }.
Dijkstra method: repeatedly finalise the lowest-cost tentative node, then relax its outgoing edges.
Forwarding method: longest matching prefix first; only then use route preference/metric rules if relevant.

comparisons.title: Routing families
rows: Send on many paths; control duplicates

solvedExamples.question: From A, direct cost to C is 9; through B it is 2+3. Which additive shortest path is chosen?
solvedExamples.solution: A→B→C, cost 5, because 5 is lower than 9.

solvedExamples.question: Routes 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.2.0.0/16 both match destination 10.2.4.9. Which forwarding entry wins?
solvedExamples.solution: 10.2.0.0/16. It has the longer, more specific prefix.

traps: Forwarding and routing are related but not identical.
BGP is inter-AS and policy-aware; it is not ordinary shortest-path routing.
RIP is distance vector; OSPF is link state.
takeaways: Forwarding uses a table; routing builds it.
Flooding needs duplicate control.
Distance vector can suffer count-to-infinity.
Link state floods topology and runs Dijkstra.
Longest prefix controls packet forwarding.

quickRecall.question: Which algorithm family can suffer count-to-infinity?
Which protocol is link-state inside an AS?
What BGP attribute helps detect/avoid AS-level loops?

topics.title: TCP and UDP
topics.oneLine: TCP provides a reliable ordered byte stream; UDP provides lightweight independent datagrams; ports let either protocol reach the right process.
topics.whyItMatters: Transport-layer MCQs commonly ask which service property is built in, what a port identifies, or why an application may choose UDP.
understandSimply: IP gets data to the right host/interface. TCP and UDP get it to the right application process using port numbers. This is multiplexing at the sender and demultiplexing at the receiver.

TCP is connection-oriented and keeps state for reliability, ordering, flow control and congestion control. UDP is connectionless and preserves individual message boundaries but does not promise delivery, ordering or duplicate removal. An application can add its own recovery over UDP if it needs to.
technicalExplanation: A socket is commonly described by an IP address plus port. A TCP connection is identified by the source IP/port and destination IP/port tuple. TCP header fields include source/destination ports, sequence and acknowledgement numbers, flags, receive window and checksum. Its base header is at least 20 bytes. UDP has source/destination ports, length and checksum; its header is 8 bytes.

TCP offers a byte stream, so application message boundaries are not automatically retained. UDP transports datagrams, so one sent datagram corresponds to one received datagram if it arrives intact. Typical choices: file transfer and web transactions need TCP's reliability; simple request/response, real-time media or DNS queries may choose UDP when low setup/overhead or application control matters.

definitions.definition: 16-bit transport identifier for an application endpoint on a host.
Endpoint identified by address and port; a connection uses two endpoints.
Many sender processes share a transport service using ports.
Receiver delivers incoming data to the process selected by protocol/port information.

steps.title: Choose a transport
steps.description: Need reliable ordered stream? Start with TCP. Need independent low-overhead messages and can tolerate/handle loss? Consider UDP.

steps.title: Deliver incoming data
steps.description: Host uses protocol and destination port (and TCP connection tuple when needed) to select the receiving socket.

steps.title: Read a header calculation
steps.description: For UDP, Length includes the 8-byte header; subtract 8 for payload.

formulasAndMethods: UDP payload length = UDP Length − 8 bytes.
TCP acknowledgement number = next byte expected, not simply the last byte received.
Socket-pair method: source IP:port + destination IP:port identifies a TCP connection.

solvedExamples.question: UDP Length is 108 bytes. How many application bytes are present?
solvedExamples.solution: 100 bytes. UDP Length includes its 8-byte header: 108−8.

solvedExamples.question: A server has IP 198.51.100.10 and port 443. Can two clients connect at once?
solvedExamples.solution: Yes. Their source IP/port pairs differ, so TCP can distinguish the connections even though destination IP/port is the same.

traps: UDP checksum/error detection does not create reliable delivery.
TCP preserves byte order, not application message boundaries.
A port identifies a process endpoint, not a physical network interface.
takeaways: IP reaches host; ports reach process.
TCP is reliable ordered byte-stream service.
UDP is connectionless datagram service.
Sockets combine address and port context.
Transport choice depends on required service, not on a simplistic “TCP is always better” rule.

quickRecall.question: Which transport preserves application message boundaries?
What does TCP ACK number name?
How large is the UDP header?

topics.title: TCP connection establishment and termination
topics.oneLine: TCP first synchronises sequence numbers with a three-way handshake, then uses acknowledgements and retransmission to maintain reliable byte delivery, and closes each direction separately.
topics.whyItMatters: Handshake and sequence-number questions are high-value because the rules are precise: SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number; a normal ACK alone does not.
understandSimply: Before TCP carries application bytes, both endpoints need to know the other's starting sequence space and confirm that the path works in both directions. The three messages are SYN, SYN+ACK and ACK.

TCP is full duplex: each endpoint can send data independently. Therefore an orderly close often has four messages: one side sends FIN, the other ACKs it, then later sends its own FIN and receives an ACK.
technicalExplanation: If a client sends SYN with sequence x, it consumes one sequence number. The server's SYN+ACK acknowledges x+1 and supplies its own initial sequence y. The final ACK acknowledges y+1. Sequence numbers count bytes in the stream; the acknowledgement number is cumulative and names the next byte expected.

If an expected ACK does not arrive before a retransmission timeout, TCP retransmits. Duplicate ACKs indicate that later data reached the receiver while something earlier appears missing; classic TCP uses three duplicate ACKs to trigger fast retransmit. The active closer enters TIME-WAIT so delayed duplicates can expire and it can retransmit the final ACK if needed. RST aborts/reset a connection and is not an orderly FIN close.

definitions.definition: TCP flag used to synchronise initial sequence numbers.
TCP flag declaring no more data from its sender.
ACK of all bytes up to the next expected byte.
Repeated ACK number, often signalling a gap.
State normally held by the active closer after final acknowledgement.

steps.title: Open
steps.description: Client SYN(x) → server SYN(y)+ACK(x+1) → client ACK(y+1).

steps.title: Transfer reliably
steps.description: Receiver sends cumulative ACKs; sender uses timers and duplicate-ACK information to recover loss.

steps.title: Close
steps.description: FIN from one direction, ACK, FIN from other direction, final ACK; the active closer waits.

formulasAndMethods: SYN and FIN each consume one sequence number.
If bytes x through x+n−1 arrive in order, the cumulative ACK is x+n.
Three-way handshake means three packets/messages, not three round trips.

solvedExamples.question: Client sends SYN with sequence 400. What ACK number appears in server SYN+ACK?
solvedExamples.solution: 401. SYN consumes one sequence number, so the server expects the next number.

solvedExamples.question: TCP receives 500 in-order bytes beginning at sequence 1000. What cumulative ACK is sent?
solvedExamples.solution: 1500, because 1500 is the next byte expected after bytes 1000 through 1499.

traps: SYN+ACK contains two controls but is one message in the normal handshake.
ACK number means next expected byte, not a count of packets.
TIME-WAIT is normally associated with active close, not merely “the server”.
takeaways: Open: SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK.
SYN/FIN consume one sequence number.
TCP acknowledgements are cumulative.
Timeout and duplicate ACKs help reveal loss.
Orderly close is directional and often four steps.

quickRecall.question: Does a plain ACK consume a sequence number?
What does three duplicate ACKs commonly trigger?
quickRecall.answer: Fast retransmit in classic TCP behaviour.

quickRecall.question: Why does TIME-WAIT exist?
quickRecall.answer: To let delayed duplicates expire and permit final-ACK retransmission.

sources.title: RFC 9293 — TCP
usedFor: Connection state, sequence and acknowledgement semantics

topics.title: Flow control and congestion control
topics.oneLine: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network; a TCP sender is limited by whichever window is smaller.
topics.whyItMatters: rwnd, advertised window, cwnd, slow start and AIMD are often tested together even though they solve two different problems.
understandSimply: A receiver has finite buffer space. It advertises how much more data it can accept; this receive window (rwnd) is flow control. A sender must avoid overflowing that receiver even if the path is otherwise empty.

A network can be congested even when the receiver is fast. TCP tracks a congestion window (cwnd) as a sender-side estimate of safe data in flight. The effective limit is the smaller of rwnd and cwnd, after accounting for bytes already outstanding.
technicalExplanation: Slow start begins conservatively but increases cwnd quickly—approximately doubling per RTT under ideal acknowledgements. At a threshold (ssthresh), congestion avoidance increases more gradually, about one MSS per RTT in the classic model. This is additive increase. Loss is treated as congestion feedback, producing multiplicative decrease (AIMD).

Classic TCP reacts differently to signals. A retransmission timeout suggests more severe loss: cwnd is reduced sharply and slow start restarts. Three duplicate ACKs suggest one gap while later packets still arrived: fast retransmit/rescovery can retransmit earlier and reduce less drastically. Exact modern algorithms vary, so focus on the principle unless a question specifies a variant.

definitions.definition: Receiver-reported capacity for additional TCP data.
Congestion window limiting sender data in flight based on network feedback.
Maximum Segment Size: maximum TCP payload usually sent in one segment.
Threshold between slow-start and congestion-avoidance behaviour.
Additive increase, multiplicative decrease.

steps.title: Find the active limit
steps.description: Compare rwnd and cwnd. Smaller value is the first limit; subtract currently unacknowledged bytes if the question asks new data now.

steps.title: Grow without loss
steps.description: Slow start grows quickly; after ssthresh, congestion avoidance grows linearly in the classic model.

steps.title: React to loss
steps.description: Timeout is treated more severely than three duplicate ACKs.

formulasAndMethods: Effective sending window ≈ min(rwnd, cwnd) − bytes in flight.
Ideal slow start: cwnd roughly doubles each RTT.
Classic congestion avoidance: cwnd grows roughly one MSS per RTT; AIMD halves/reduces on congestion feedback.

solvedExamples.question: rwnd = 24 KB, cwnd = 16 KB, bytes in flight = 4 KB. How much new data can be sent?
solvedExamples.solution: min(24,16)−4 = 12 KB, assuming no other limits. cwnd is the smaller total-flight limit.

solvedExamples.question: Starting at 1 MSS, what is cwnd after three ideal slow-start RTTs with no loss?
solvedExamples.solution: Approximately 8 MSS: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8.

traps: A zero receive window means receiver pressure, not necessarily network congestion.
rwnd and cwnd are not interchangeable.
Slow start is fast growth, not a slow linear increase.
takeaways: Flow control protects the receiver.
Congestion control protects the network.
Effective send amount is constrained by min(rwnd, cwnd).
Slow start grows roughly exponentially by RTT.
Timeout generally signals more severe congestion than duplicate ACKs.

quickRecall.question: Which window is advertised by the receiver?
What does cwnd try to protect?
Which event is usually treated as more severe: timeout or three duplicate ACKs?

sources.title: RFC 5681 — TCP Congestion Control
usedFor: Classic slow start, congestion avoidance and loss response

topics.title: DNS, HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP and email
topics.oneLine: Application protocols turn network transport into useful services: naming, web exchange, files and email.
topics.whyItMatters: These questions often test role confusion—DNS versus DHCP, SMTP versus IMAP/POP3, HTTP versus HTTPS, or FTP's two connections.
understandSimply: DNS is the Internet's distributed naming system. It translates names into records such as IPv4/IPv6 addresses. A resolver can answer from cache or walk delegations from root to top-level domain to authoritative server.

HTTP is a stateless request-response protocol for web resources. HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS; TLS provides a secure channel with server authentication and integrity/confidentiality protections when configured correctly.
technicalExplanation: A non-persistent HTTP connection carries one request/response before it closes; persistent HTTP reuses a connection for multiple resources, reducing setup overhead. Common exam ports: DNS 53, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, FTP control 21, SMTP 25. Treat ports as defaults, not proof of protocol identity.

FTP uses separate TCP control and data connections. SMTP transfers mail between client/server and mail servers. POP3 mainly downloads messages for client access; IMAP keeps/manages mail on the server. A normal email path is sender MUA → sender mail server using SMTP → recipient mail server using SMTP → recipient reads through IMAP or POP3.

definitions.definition: Server holding final data for a DNS zone.
Resolver that obtains a complete DNS answer on behalf of a client.
Request semantic such as GET or POST.
Connection reused for multiple HTTP exchanges.
Mail User Agent, the user's email client.

steps.title: Resolve a web name
steps.description: Browser asks resolver; cache may answer. Otherwise resolver follows root, TLD and authoritative delegation to obtain a record.

steps.title: Fetch over HTTPS
steps.description: Client establishes secure transport with TLS, then exchanges HTTP requests/responses inside it.

steps.title: Deliver email
steps.description: Sender client submits by SMTP; servers relay by SMTP; recipient client reads using IMAP or POP3.

formulasAndMethods: Role method: names → DNS; web request/response → HTTP; secure web channel → HTTPS/TLS; file-control/data channels → FTP; mail transfer → SMTP; mailbox access → IMAP/POP3.
Port memory aid: 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 21 FTP control, 25 SMTP.

solvedExamples.question: Which record maps example.com to an IPv4 address?
solvedExamples.solution: An A record. AAAA is for an IPv6 address; MX identifies mail-exchange routing.

solvedExamples.question: Which protocol normally moves mail from one mail server to another, and which commonly lets a user access a mailbox?
solvedExamples.solution: SMTP transfers the mail. IMAP or POP3 provides mailbox access; SMTP is not the usual reading protocol.

traps: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS, not a new language or a guarantee that a page is trustworthy.
DNS can use UDP or TCP; it is not “UDP only”.
SMTP transfers mail; IMAP/POP3 retrieve/manage it.
takeaways: DNS hierarchy resolves names to records.
HTTP is request-response and stateless by design.
HTTPS adds TLS protection to HTTP.
FTP has separate control and data channels.
SMTP moves mail; IMAP/POP3 access mailboxes.

quickRecall.question: Which DNS record carries an IPv6 address?
What is the default HTTPS port?
Which email protocol transfers mail between servers?

topics.title: Network security fundamentals
topics.oneLine: Security asks what must be protected—secrecy, correctness and availability—and which control provides it.
topics.whyItMatters: This is a lower-priority foundation topic for this module, but basic CIA, crypto and security-control distinctions prevent easy conceptual errors.
understandSimply: Confidentiality means unauthorised people cannot read data. Integrity means unauthorised changes are detected or prevented. Availability means a service remains usable. Authentication answers “who/what is this?”; authorization answers “what may it do?”

Security tools have different jobs. Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret and is efficient for data. Asymmetric cryptography uses a public/private key pair for identity, key establishment and signatures. A hash is a one-way digest; it is not encrypted text that can be decrypted.
technicalExplanation: A digital signature typically signs a hash with the sender's private key; anyone with the sender's public key can verify integrity and data origin. It does not itself hide the message. TLS is a protocol suite used by HTTPS to establish a protected channel; it combines authenticated key establishment with symmetric protection of application data.

A firewall applies traffic policy, for example allowing or blocking flows. An IDS detects suspicious activity and alerts; an IPS is placed to actively block/prevent according to policy. At exam depth, recognise phishing/social engineering, malware, password guessing and denial-of-service as examples, then map the harmed security goal rather than memorising a long attack catalogue.

definitions.definition: Protection against unauthorised disclosure.
Protection against unauthorised modification or destruction.
Verification of identity or data origin.
Asymmetric mechanism for integrity and origin authentication.
Intrusion Detection System alerts; Intrusion Prevention System can actively block.

steps.title: Classify the goal
steps.description: Disclosure → confidentiality; silent change → integrity; outage → availability; identity claim → authentication.

steps.title: Choose the primitive
steps.description: Bulk secrecy → symmetric encryption; verify origin/integrity → signature; fixed digest → hash.

steps.title: Read HTTPS correctly
steps.description: TLS establishes/protects the channel; HTTP semantics then travel inside that protected channel.

formulasAndMethods: Signature method: hash message → sign using sender private key → verify using sender public key.
Security-goal method: disclosure / modification / outage map to confidentiality / integrity / availability.

solvedExamples.question: An attacker silently changes a routing update. Which CIA goal is directly violated?
solvedExamples.solution: Integrity. The information was modified without authorisation.

solvedExamples.question: Which key verifies Alice's digital signature?
solvedExamples.solution: Alice's public key. Alice signs with her private key; verifiers must not need her secret private key.

traps: Hashing is not reversible encryption.
A digital signature does not provide confidentiality by itself.
Authentication and authorization answer different questions.
takeaways: CIA means confidentiality, integrity and availability.
Symmetric crypto is efficient for bulk data.
Public/private keys support signatures and key establishment.
Sign with private key; verify with public key.
Firewall, IDS and IPS have different enforcement roles.

quickRecall.question: Which CIA goal is harmed by a service outage?
Does a signature hide the message?
quickRecall.answer: No; it provides integrity and origin authentication, not confidentiality by itself.

quickRecall.question: How does IPS differ from IDS?
quickRecall.answer: IDS detects/alerts; IPS can actively block or prevent.
